flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx: "To return multiple elements from a component, wrap them with a single parent tag." The same page adds: "You can't return two objects from a function without wrapping them into an array." A component may legally return an array of keyed sibling elements (the deck's own sr6-01 says "A component renders an array of JSX elements returned by map()"), so "sibling JSX elements" do not have to sit under a single root. The statement also reads as a description of what a component does instead of naming the rule and who applies it.
flagged.problem: An expert could answer False, because returning an array of keyed siblings is valid React with no single root element. The rule the docs teach is about adjacent JSX tags, and the statement does not say that.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer true): "Two adjacent JSX tags in a component's return need a wrapping parent tag or Fragment to compile." Explanation: "JSX compiles to JavaScript objects, and a function cannot return two values at once, so adjacent tags need one parent such as a <div> or <>...</>." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx: "Since class is a reserved word, in React you write className instead, named after the corresponding DOM property" and "If you get one wrong, don't worry, React will print a message with a possible correction to the browser console." React DOM still passes class through to the element with a development warning. https://legacy.reactjs.org/blog/2017/09/08/dom-attributes-in-react-16.html, on known attributes with a different canonical React name such as class: "React 16: Warns but converts values to strings and passes them through." That behaviour has not been removed in React 19.
flagged.problem: Read literally ("uses the HTML class attribute to assign a CSS class to a DOM node"), the statement describes something that works at runtime with a console warning, so an expert could defend True. The fact being tested is the documented naming convention, and the statement should say so.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer false): "React's documentation writes a DOM element's CSS class in JSX with the HTML attribute name class." Explanation: "Because class is a reserved word in JavaScript, the docs write className, named after the DOM property; React prints a console warning when it sees class." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces: "You can only use curly braces in two ways inside JSX: As text directly inside a JSX tag ... As attributes immediately following the = sign: src={avatar} will read the avatar variable, but src="{avatar}" will pass the string "{avatar}"." The card only restates the basic definition of curly braces in JSX. No one who has studied would answer False, so it teaches nothing at its difficulty 2. Read literally it is also loose: braces inside a quoted attribute are not evaluated, and braces in an attribute give a value, not element content.
flagged.problem: This is a near-definition card: the answer follows from what curly braces in JSX are. The page has a sharper fact that tests the same sub-topic.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer true): "In JSX, src=\"{avatar}\" passes the literal text {avatar} rather than the avatar variable's value." Explanation: "Quotes make an attribute a string, so the braces are plain text. To read the variable, write src={avatar} with the braces right after the = sign." Keep the same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component: "Props are the information that you pass to a JSX tag." The statement restates what a prop is, so it is a definition card. A developer who ships React daily (the depth the prompt sets) cannot answer False, so the card teaches nothing.
flagged.problem: This is a definition card and a truism: passing a prop as an attribute on the child's JSX tag is what a prop is. The answer follows from the meaning of the term.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps True). Statement: "A mounted component can receive different prop values from its parent on later renders." Explanation: "Props reflect the parent's data at each render: a Clock's time prop can change every second while the same Clock stays mounted." Same URL ("a component may receive different props over time. Props are not always static!"). If adopted, shorten sr2-06's explanation to "Props are read-only snapshots; a component that needs a different value asks its parent to pass new props." so it stays on its own fact.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component: "React component functions accept a single argument, a props object" and "This syntax is called 'destructuring' and is equivalent to reading properties from a function parameter." Destructuring { person, size } in the parameter only works because the component receives one props object, which is the fact sr2-02 tests.
flagged.problem: Same fact as sr2-02 (component-props-object-argument). Knowing that props are destructured in the single parameter answers sr2-02 (props are not separate positional arguments), and the reverse also holds. It is also close to a truism for the audience.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps True). Statement: "A parent can pass a JSX element to a child through a prop other than children, such as icon={<Star />}." Explanation: "Props accept any JavaScript value, and a JSX element is a value, so a component can render a received icon prop wherever it places {icon}." Same URL ("you can pass any JavaScript value through them, including objects, arrays, and functions").

sections.notes: I checked all 12 r2 cards (sr2-01 to sr2-12) from react-fundamentals-b1.json. The split is 6 true and 6 false. Every source URL loads (HTTP 200) on react.dev, and the pages show v19.3. Sources that settle the passing cards: - passing-props-to-a-component, default value for null: "The default value is only used if the size prop is missing or if you pass size={undefined}. But if you pass size={null} or size={0}, the default value will not be used." This settles sr2-04 (False). - Same page, children: "When you nest content inside a JSX tag, the parent component will receive that content in a prop called children." This settles sr2-05. - Same page, read-only props: "props are immutable", "Props are read-only snapshots in time". This settles sr2-06 (False). - Same page, spread: " ... forwards all of Profile's props". This settles sr2-08. - Same page, custom props: "The props you can pass to an tag are predefined ... But you can pass any props to your own components". This settles sr2-09 (False). - forwardRef page: "In React 19, forwardRef is no longer necessary. Pass ref as a prop instead." This settles sr2-10. The React 19 post is stronger: "Starting in React 19, you can now access ref as a prop for function components." - Upgrade guide: "We're also removing defaultProps from function components in place of ES6 default parameters. Class components will continue to support defaultProps". This settles sr2-11 (False). - Upgrade guide: "In React 19, we're removing the propType checks from the React package, and using them will be silently ignored." This settles sr2-12 (False). The removal covers class components too, so the "function components" wording is still false. I found no answer errors and no version problems. Every card that depends on a React 19 change names React 19 in its statement. Borderline cards I let pass: - sr2-07 (callback functions as props): very easy for the target audience, but React-specific and not wrong. sr2-10-04 tests a different fact (Effect versus event for notifying a parent). - sr2-09 and sr2-02: the false misconceptions are weak but documented. The page contrasts props with HTML attributes and says "props are the only argument". - sr2-06: an expert could note that mutating a nested object prop does change the parent's object. Still, it neither updates nor re-renders the parent, and React freezes the props object in development, so False holds. - sr2-11 and sr2-12 come from the same upgrade-guide heading but test separate facts. On the forwardRef page, the 19.3 docs now list forwardRef under Legacy APIs with a "Deprecated" badge, while its text says it "will be deprecated in a future release". sr2-10 avoids that claim, so it is fine. Other sections: no duplicates found. sr6-10 (key), sr7-12 (children before context) and sr14-07 (JSX prop across the server/client boundary) test different facts. If the sr2-03 replacement is adopted, it sits close to sr14-07, but the facts differ.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, official react.dev page, current (site header shows React v19.3)
flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit: "it's done by calling createRoot with the target DOM node, and then calling its render method with your component". The fact is right, but you can read the answer straight off the method name: root.render 'triggers the initial render'. The explanation is also slightly misleading. It says "createRoot selects a DOM container", but the developer passes the node in, and createRoot does not select it.
flagged.problem: Name giveaway that a player can guess without knowing React (a method called render starts the render). The explanation wrongly makes createRoot the actor that picks the container.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (true): "On a re-render, React first calls the component whose state update triggered it rather than the root component." Explanation: "Only the initial render starts at the root component. For later renders, React begins with the component whose state changed and then renders the components it returns." Source: https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit ("For subsequent renders, React will call the function component whose state update triggered the render.")

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit: "Updating your component's state automatically queues a render." The card is correct. However, react-fundamentals-sr8-02 ("Changing ref.current requests a component re-render like a state setter", false) tests the other side of the same state-versus-ref split and even states this card's fact as its premise.
flagged.problem: The prompt treats the two sides of one distinction as one fact. sr3-02 (a state update queues a render) and sr8-02 (a ref change does not, unlike a state setter) mirror each other. On its own it is also close to a truism for working React developers.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (true): "During a re-render, React calculates which DOM properties changed and waits until the commit phase to apply them." Explanation: "Rendering only calculates the difference from the previous render. React touches the DOM in the commit step, applying the minimal operations needed to match the new output." Source: https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit ("During a re-render, React will calculate which of their properties, if any, have changed... It won't do anything with that information until the next step, the commit phase."). Or keep this card and rewrite sr8-02 instead.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree: "With conditional rendering, across different renders, the render tree may render different components." The answer is right. But no learner who knows what conditional rendering is would claim the tree keeps the same shape across branches, so 'hard' (difficulty 3) is unjustified. The same page has a stronger fact: "the render tree is only composed of React components".
flagged.problem: Strawman. The answer follows from the meaning of 'conditional rendering', and the awkward wording ('component shape across conditional branches') adds no real distinction.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (false): "React's render tree has a node for each HTML element a component returns, such as div or img." Explanation: "The render tree is composed only of React components. Host elements such as div or img are platform UI primitives, so React leaves them out of the render tree." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree: "Non-component modules, like inspirations.js, are also represented in this tree. The render tree only encapsulates components." Correct, but a 'module dependency tree' holds every imported module by definition. The page's real teaching point about how the two trees differ is: "Copyright.js appears under App.js but in the render tree, Copyright, the component, appears as a child of InspirationGenerator... because InspirationGenerator accepts JSX as children props".
flagged.problem: Definition card: you can get the answer from the term 'module dependency tree'. It also says nothing React-specific.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (true): "In the render tree, a component passed as children sits under its renderer rather than its importer." Explanation: "If App imports Copyright but passes it as children to InspirationGenerator, the render tree puts Copyright under InspirationGenerator while the module dependency tree puts it under App." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure: "Components must always return the same output with respect to their inputs – props, state, and context. This is known as idempotency." The statement just negates the definition of a pure component. The page also gives a concrete, testable case: "functions like Math.random() also aren't idempotent, because they return different results every time they're called".
flagged.problem: Definition card / strawman. Anyone who knows the word 'pure' answers False without knowing anything about React.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (false): "Reading Math.random() while rendering keeps a component pure because it changes no existing variable." Explanation: "Purity also means idempotency: the same props, state and context must give the same JSX. Math.random() and new Date() return new values each call, so use them outside render." Same URL.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure: "If the cups variable or the [] array were created outside the TeaGathering function, this would be a huge problem!... However, it's fine because you've created them during the same render". This one sentence settles both sr3-10 (local array, true) and sr3-11 (preexisting array, false).
flagged.problem: It rests on the same fact as react-fundamentals-sr3-10 (local versus non-local mutation during render): knowing one answer gives you the other. The prompt forbids testing both sides of one distinction.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (false): "A component can safely mutate an object it created during render after passing that object to JSX." Explanation: "React may evaluate JSX eagerly, so mutating a value after using it in JSX can leave an outdated UI. Make the change before creating the JSX, or create a new object." Source: https://react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure ("Don't mutate values after they've been used in JSX. Move the mutation to before the JSX is created.")

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure: "Side effects should not run in render, as React can render components multiple times". The rule is a prohibition, not an impossibility: JavaScript code in render can physically send an analytics request. The statement's "can send" can be read as capability, which is true, or as permission, which is false.
flagged.problem: An expert could defend True on the capability reading of 'can' (it runs, it just breaks the Rules of React). In a false statement the hedge verb opens a technicality.
flagged.suggestedFix: Reword (false): "The Rules of React allow a component to send an analytics event while it renders." Explanation: "Sending an analytics event is a side effect. React may render a component several times, so side effects belong in event handlers or, as a last resort, in an Effect." Same URL.

sections.notes:
I checked all 12 r3 cards (all in react-fundamentals-b1.json). Every source URL returned 200 and is the current react.dev page; the site header shows React v19.3. Pages: /learn/render-and-commit, /learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree, /learn/keeping-components-pure, /reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure. None of the r3 answers is factually wrong, and none depends on a React 19 minor version, so 'React 19' in appliesTo is right throughout.

Cards that pass:
- sr3-03: "'Rendering' is React calling your components." This is borderline as a definition card, but it teaches the docs' mental model that rendering is not a DOM update.
- sr3-04: "The default behavior of rendering all components nested within the updated component". An expert might raise React skipping an element passed in unchanged as children, or React Compiler, but neither makes skipping the default for a parent's own JSX.
- sr3-05: "For the initial render, React will use the appendChild() DOM API to put all the DOM nodes it has created on screen". This is weak and close to a truism; difficulty 2 is generous.
- sr3-06: "React does not touch the DOM if the rendering result is the same as last time".
- sr3-10: the local mutation passage.

The flags are mostly about quality, not wrong answers:
- One name giveaway (01).
- Two definition or strawman cards (07, 09) and one definition card (08).
- Two duplicates: sr3-10/11 are both sides of local versus non-local mutation, and sr3-02 mirrors sr8-02 (state versus ref triggering a render). If the deck owner prefers, the second one can be fixed by rewriting sr8-02 instead.
- One capability-versus-permission ambiguity in 12.

Balance after the suggested replacements: 6 true (01 new, 02 new, 03, 05, 08 new, 10) and 6 false (04, 06, 07 new, 09 new, 11 new, 12 reworded). Average statement length is 94.2 for true and 89.3 for false, a gap of 4.9 characters, just within the 5-character rule. If sr3-05 is also replaced, use a shorter true statement. Every replacement is 120 characters or less, its explanation 240 or less, and it uses no negation or absolute.

flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates: "setNumber(number + 5): number is 0, so setNumber(0 + 5). React adds 'replace with 5' to its queue." and "You may have noticed that setState(5) actually works like setState(n => 5), but n is unused!" The page supports the answer (false) and the explanation.
flagged.problem: Strawman. The answer and source are correct, but the misconception (a plain number passed to a setter is added to the queued value) is not one a developer who uses React holds. Every reset such as setCount(0) shows that a plain value replaces the state. The queueing lesson is easy to misread in other ways, but nobody who studied it reads 'replace with 5' as 'add 5'.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace, keeping the answer false. Statement (82 chars): "Passing a function to a state setter stores that function as the new state value." Explanation: "React treats a function passed to a set function as an updater and calls it. To store a function in state, wrap it, for example setFn(() => someFunction)." Source: https://react.dev/reference/react/useState ("If you pass a function as nextState, it will be treated as an updater function." and the troubleshooting entry "I'm trying to set state to a function, but it gets called instead"). flagged.evidence: https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state: "State is tied to a position in the render tree" supports the intended answer, but the same page also says of keyed components: "React will know Taylor's counter wherever it appears in the tree!" and "Specifying a key tells React to use the key itself as part of the position, instead of their order within the parent." https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists likewise says keys let React keep track of an item even if its position changes, for example after a reorder.

Statement (103 chars): "Without a key, a component's state follows its JSX tag when the tag moves to a different tree position." Explanation (160 chars): "React ties state to a component's position in the render tree, not to its JSX tag, so an unkeyed component rendered at another position starts with fresh state."

Recap: "It's useful to consider components as 'controlled' (driven by props) or 'uncontrolled' (driven by state)."
